paragraphs.heading: A new star that isn't
paragraphs.text: A nova is a sudden event in which a bright, seemingly new star appears in the sky and then fades slowly over weeks or months. The name is Latin for new, short for stella nova, meaning new star. In past centuries people did think such an event was a new star. In fact novae most often happen on white dwarfs, which are the remnants of extremely old stars.

paragraphs.heading: Two stars, one feeding the other
paragraphs.text: Every observed nova involves a white dwarf in a close binary system. The story begins with two main sequence stars in a binary. One evolves into a red giant and leaves its white dwarf core still orbiting the other star. When that second star overflows its Roche lobe, it starts to shed its outer envelope onto the white dwarf. The white dwarf gathers this matter in an accretion disk, and from there it falls into the white dwarf's atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Runaway fusion
paragraphs.text: The captured gas, mostly hydrogen, builds a dense but shallow atmosphere on the white dwarf, which heats it. Because the white dwarf is made of degenerate matter, the hydrogen cannot expand even as it grows hotter. When the layer reaches about 20 million K, runaway fusion starts through the CNO cycle. The sudden burst of energy blows the gas out into space, and that envelope is the bright light seen as the nova.

paragraphs.heading: Surprisingly little matter
paragraphs.text: For all its violence, a nova usually throws off only about 1⁄10,000 of a solar mass, which is small next to the white dwarf's own mass. Only five percent of the accreted matter is fused in the outburst. That is still enough to fling the ejected gas outward at up to several thousand kilometers per second. Meanwhile the nova's luminosity climbs from a few times the Sun's to 50,000–100,000 times. In 2010 NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope found that a nova can also emit gamma rays.

paragraphs.heading: Again and again
paragraphs.text: A white dwarf can produce many novae over time, because hydrogen keeps arriving from its companion. When the flaring is seen to repeat, the object is called a recurrent nova. RS Ophiuchi is one: it has erupted seven times, the earliest in 1898 and the latest listed in 2021. If the white dwarf approaches the Chandrasekhar limit, it can instead blow up as a Type Ia supernova, which destroys the white dwarf rather than just expelling its atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Watching for novae
paragraphs.text: About ten novae happen each year in the Milky Way, far more often than supernovae in our galaxy. Most are found with telescopes; perhaps one every 12–18 months becomes visible to the naked eye. They turn up most often along the band of the Milky Way across the sky, above all toward the Galactic Center in Sagittarius, but they can appear anywhere in the sky. The last bright nova was V1369 Centauri, which reached magnitude 3.3 on 14 December 2013.
